accuracy.evidence: Comparison language checked against Development Matters 2021 (3 and 4 year olds compare quantities using language such as more than and fewer than) and the Reception ELG for number (compare quantities up to 10, recognising when one quantity is greater than, less than or the same as the other). Every round has a correct answer that the matching or counting on screen proves; 'fewer' is used for countable things as the guidance does.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the Piagetian conservation errors seen at this age: the longer spread-out row judged to have more, squashed cars judged to have fewer, three big apples judged more than five small grapes, and near counts (3 vs 4) judged the same. Each of these appears as a prediction, a lab round and a tagged wrong option in the challenge.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagmore uses its own mechanics: draw a line from each of Mia's cars to one of Leo's to find the one left over, tap-count with big numerals over each item, and a plus/minus plate to make two sets equal, then a fewer round. No other flag lab pairs items one-to-one; the 6-token shingle gate passed against all flag labs.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child sees the reason: the spare car without a partner stays unlinked and is named, counting numbers appear 1 to 5 over the tiny beads to beat the big balls, and the plate only says 'the same' when the counts match. Text only confirms what the matching or counting already showed.

predictions.evidence: Two locked predictions before the reveal: whether the longer spread-out row has more cars (it does not, the squashed row has a spare), and whether 3 big balls beat 5 tiny beads (they do not). Each tempting wrong answer is offered first and then disproved on screen.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating challenge questions with tagged wrong answers: 'less' explains 4 is more than 3, 'near' says close is not the same and a spare is left, 'long' and 'short' say spreading or squashing does not change how many, 'big' says more means more things, and 'one' works out that Mia needs 2 more not 1.

readability.evidence: Family audience: validate_lessons readability passes with kid text at FK -0.7 and adult text at FK 7.1. Kid sentences are a few words long with names, grapes, cars and cookies; the adult text uses exact terms: compare, more than, fewer than, the same as, one-to-one correspondence and conservation of number.

no_filler.evidence: The filler gate found no stock phrases and explanation overlap with other lessons stays under 12 percent. Each kid paragraph is one idea with a concrete pair of groups; adult paragraphs give the goals, the matching strategy, named mistakes and what each lab step does.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360x640 Android light and dark and iPhone 13 light for all six steps: two tall coloured rows for Mia and Leo, big buttons in a single column, numerals legible over items. Squashed cars were overlapping at 360 px; spacing and car width were changed and rechecked. walk.cjs passes on desktop and iPhone 13.

accessibility.evidence: axe reports no violations in light or dark; every action has a button (Match a pair, Count Mia's, + give Mia one) besides drag, the canvas aria-label is updated with each spoken result, and Show me completes every task within 6 seconds. Colours are paired with names and counts, never colour alone.

sources: DfE (2021) Development Matters: Mathematics, comparing quantities (3 and 4 year olds; Reception)
DfE (2021) Statutory framework for the EYFS: ELG Number and Numerical Patterns (compare quantities up to 10)
NCETM Early Years: comparison and conservation of number; Piaget number conservation tasks
